story.headline: Oil climbed toward $114 a barrel, near its highest since May, as Houthi attacks forced Saudi Aramco to clear its headquarters. The yen hit a one-month high, and UK retail sales fell more than expected.

reads.policy: Almost every major central bank still leans toward raising rates because high oil keeps inflation up. A stock-market scare has trimmed bets on a December Federal Reserve hike, which takes a little support from the dollar. Switzerland remains the odd one out.
reads.growth: Households are starting to pull back where energy bills bite hardest. UK shoppers spent less and their confidence slumped, and Australia's private sector shrank. Weaker growth makes it harder for those central banks to keep raising rates.
reads.inflation: Energy keeps inflation high almost everywhere, which is why so many central banks lean toward hikes. Japan's inflation is back above the Bank of Japan's goal and spreading beyond fuel, which strengthens the case for a December hike there and helps the yen.
reads.risk: Investors are nervous: worries about AI spending keep hitting tech shares, and attacks on Saudi Arabia add to the unease. Money is going into US government bonds and the yen, while gold keeps sliding instead of acting as a shelter.
reads.tot: Oil is near its highest since May as Houthi attacks reach deeper into Saudi Arabia and Libyan output dips. That helps exporters like Canada and hurts big energy importers like Japan and the euro area.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds are betting most heavily against the Canadian dollar, even as a Bank of Canada hike looks likely, which leaves those bets exposed if the loonie keeps rising. They also bet against the kiwi and the euro. In the yen and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.
reads.fiscal: Government finances are weighing on the euro: France pays more than 5% to borrow for ten years, near its widest gap over Germany since 2011. Moody's reviews France's rating tonight, and Britain's budget follows on October 28, with shoppers already holding back ahead of it.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve is expected to hold rates on October 28 and raise them in December, because high oil keeps US inflation up. A stock-market scare has made that December hike look a little less certain, taking some shine off the dollar.
fed.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
fed.why: Energy-driven inflation is still too high for the Fed's comfort and layoffs are rare, but falling stocks and bond yields ease the pressure to keep tightening.
fed.watch: Friday's US business surveys and the University of Michigan's inflation expectations, then the decision on October 28. The Fed is in its quiet period until then.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada is expected to raise rates on October 28 after governor Tiff Macklem warned that energy will push inflation well above the bank's forecasts. Much of that is already in the Canadian dollar's price.
boc.why: High oil is lifting Canadian inflation, and factory and raw material prices jumped far more than expected in September.
boc.watch: Canadian retail sales on Friday, then whether the bank signals more hikes after October 28; a hold would be the surprise.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is expected to raise rates on October 28. Inflation cooled slightly in the third quarter but stayed above the bank's target, so the hike case held and supports the kiwi.
rbnz.priced: October 28: hike near certain; a second hike by February fully priced.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the bank's 1–3% target band, and core prices stayed firm even as the headline eased.
rbnz.watch: Whether the bank signals a run of hikes at its October 28 decision, or sounds content after one.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank is expected to hold on October 29 and lean toward a hike in December, as energy keeps euro-area inflation high. That supports the euro, but France's debt worries pull the other way.
ecb.priced: October 29: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Expensive energy is keeping euro-area inflation well above target, but gloomier households and France's rising borrowing costs argue for caution.
ecb.watch: Friday's business surveys and Moody's review of France, then what President Christine Lagarde says about December on October 29.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on October 30, but a December hike is increasingly expected now that inflation is back above its 2% goal. The yen needs that hike, or clear signals of it, to recover.
boj.priced: October 30: hold expected; December: hike likely.
boj.why: Japan's inflation rose back above 2% in September and is spreading beyond fuel, the evidence the bank has said it needs.
boj.watch: Whether governor Kazuo Ueda signals a December hike at the October 29–30 meeting, and whether the bank raises its inflation forecast.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia may raise rates on November 3, with markets seeing it as close to an even bet. Weak business surveys have made the call harder, which caps the Australian dollar.
rba.priced: November 3: hike close to even odds; December: hike more likely than not.
rba.why: Rising costs and deputy governor Andrew Hauser's warning on inflation argue for a hike, but a shrinking private sector argues for waiting.
rba.watch: Australia's third-quarter inflation figures on October 28, the last big input before the November decision.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is all but certain to raise rates on November 5 after UK inflation came in hotter than expected. Weak shopping and a slump in consumer confidence make a second hike in December less likely, which weighs on the pound.
boe.priced: November 5: hike near certain; December: second hike a coin toss.
boe.why: Energy is pushing UK inflation far above the 2% target, but households are now cutting back ahead of the budget.
boe.watch: UK business surveys on Friday and the October 28 budget, which may add help with energy bills.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds rates at zero because Swiss inflation is near zero. It has said it is comfortable with a weaker franc and no longer stands as ready to intervene, so global fear sets the franc's path.
snb.priced: December 10: hold expected; markets split on the next move.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is barely above zero, and a strong franc keeps import prices low, so the bank sees no need to tighten.
snb.watch: Swiss inflation figures in early November, and any sign the bank is ready to cut or step into currency markets.

USD.summary: The dollar has the highest rates among the major currencies, with a Federal Reserve hike expected in December, but a rush into US bonds has pulled yields down and left it near a three-week low.

notes.policy: The Fed is expected to hold in October and hike in December, though a stock-market scare has trimmed those bets a little.
notes.inflation: High oil keeps US inflation well above the Fed's goal, which supports the case for more hikes.

EUR.summary: The euro is held back by expensive energy and France's rising borrowing costs, and the European Central Bank is moving more slowly than the US and UK central banks.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank is expected to hold in October and is behind the Fed and the Bank of England in raising rates, which gives the euro less support.
notes.growth: The euro-area economy looks weaker than the US, with households gloomier and France's political strain weighing on it.
notes.inflation: Energy keeps euro-area inflation well above target, which pushes the central bank toward a hike.
notes.tot: Europe imports most of its energy, so high oil and gas prices drain money out of the region.
notes.fiscal: France pays more than 5% to borrow for ten years, and Moody's reviews its credit rating on Friday.

GBP.summary: The pound is supported by a Bank of England hike in November that is all but certain after hot UK inflation, though weak shopping and gloomy consumers cloud the case for more.

notes.policy: A Bank of England hike on November 5 is nearly fully priced, with a second in December a coin toss.
notes.growth: UK jobs have stayed strong, but shoppers cut back in September and confidence slumped in October.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is running far above the 2% target, driven by energy.

JPY.summary: The yen is still weak because Japan's rates are far below everyone else's, but it is at its strongest in over a month as stock-market fears send investors to safety.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rates are far below other major banks', though a December hike is increasingly expected.
notes.risk: The yen is a safe place to park money, so it gains when stock markets fall.
notes.tot: Japan imports most of its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country and weighs on the yen.

CHF.summary: The franc is held between two forces: it gains when fear rises, but near-zero Swiss inflation keeps the central bank from raising rates.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is near zero, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates and may cut.
notes.risk: The franc is a safe place to park money, so it tends to gain when the Gulf conflict flares or stocks fall.

AUD.summary: The Australian dollar is supported by the chance of a Reserve Bank of Australia hike in November, but a shrinking private sector has made that call harder.

notes.policy: Markets see close to even odds of a Reserve Bank of Australia hike on November 3.
notes.growth: Australia's private sector shrank in October for the first time in five months, which tempers the case for hikes.
notes.tot: Firm prices for Australia's exports bring money into the country and support the currency.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar is near its strongest in a month, supported by high oil and a Bank of Canada hike expected on October 28.

notes.policy: A Bank of Canada hike on October 28 is mostly priced.
notes.growth: Canada's housing and shopping figures have been soft, which could limit how far the bank goes after October.
notes.inflation: Factory and raw material prices jumped far more than expected, a sign more inflation is coming.
notes.tot: High oil lifts Canada's export income, which supports the currency.

NZD.summary: The kiwi is supported by a Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on October 28 that markets see as near certain, but it falls hard when war and tech fears hit stock markets.

notes.policy: A Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on October 28 is close to fully priced, with more expected by February.
notes.growth: New Zealand's factories are having their best stretch since 2021, giving the central bank room to raise rates.
notes.risk: Steady demand from China and a softer US dollar have helped the kiwi this month, though it still drops when stocks fall.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
